def solve():
    # The problem asks for the smallest M such that any M flags contain 8 flags forming a diverse set.
    # A set of 8 flags F is diverse if it has a Y-perfect matching or a B-perfect matching.
    # S contains no diverse set if every F \subseteq S of size 8 has neither a Y-perfect matching nor a B-perfect matching.
    # S has no Y-perfect matching if \exists I \subseteq {1..8} such that |N_Y(I) \cap S| < |I|.
    # S has no B-perfect matching if \exists J \subseteq {1..8} such that |N_B(J) \cap S| < |J|.
    # These conditions must hold for S because if S has a Y-perfect matching, it would contain a Y-diverse 8-subset.
    # Let k = |I| and l = |J|.
    # The condition |N_Y(I) \cap S| < k means that at least |S| - k + 1 flags in S have B at all positions in I.
    # The condition |N_B(J) \cap S| < l means that at least |S| - l + 1 flags in S have Y at all positions in J.
    # Let S_I be the set of flags in S having B at all positions in I.
    # Let S_J be the set of flags in S having Y at all positions in J.
    # Then |S_I| >= |S| - k + 1 and |S_J| >= |S| - l + 1.
    # Also, since I and J must be disjoint (otherwise S_I \cap S_J would be empty),
    # the flags in S_I \cap S_J have B at all positions in I and Y at all positions in J.
    # The number of such flags is 2^{8-k-l}.
    # So |S_I \cap S_J| <= 2^{8-k-l}.
    # Since S_I and S_J are subsets of S, |S_I \cup S_J| <= |S|.
    # By inclusion-exclusion, |S_I \cup S_J| = |S_I| + |S_J| - |S_I \cap S_J|.
    # So |S| >= |S_I| + |S_J| - |S_I \cap S_J| >= (|S| - k + 1) + (|S| - l + 1) - 2^{8-k-l}.
    # |S| >= 2|S| - k - l + 2 - 2^{8-k-l}
    # |S| <= k + l - 2 + 2^{8-k-l}.
    # We want to maximize |S| over k, l >= 1 such that k+l <= 8.
    # k=1, l=1: |S| <= 1 + 1 - 2 + 2^6 = 64.
    # k=2, l=1: |S| <= 2 + 1 - 2 + 2^5 = 33.
    # k=2, l=2: |S| <= 2 + 2 - 2 + 2^4 = 18.
    # The maximum is 64.
    # Thus M = 64 + 1 = 65.
    print(65)

solve()

log.content:
The problem asks for the smallest positive integer $M$ such that any set of $M$ distinct flags contains a "diverse" set of 8 flags. A set of 8 flags is diverse if it can be arranged into an $8 \times 8$ square such that all 8 fields on its main diagonal have the same color (either all yellow or all blue).

Let $S$ be a set of flags. A subset $F \subseteq S$ of size 8 is diverse if there exists a permutation of its flags $\sigma$ such that the elements on the main diagonal are all the same color $c$. This is equivalent to the existence of a perfect matching in a bipartite graph $G_c$ where an edge exists between position $i \in \{1, \dots, 8\}$ and flag $f \in F$ if the $i$-th component of $f$ is color $c$.

By Hall's Marriage Theorem, $G_c$ has no perfect matching if and only if there exists a subset of positions $I \subseteq \{1, \dots, 8\}$ such that $|N_c(I)| < |I|$, where $N_c(I)$ is the set of flags in $F$ having color $c$ at any position in $I$.
A set $S$ contains no diverse set of 8 flags if and only if every $F \subseteq S$ of size 8 has no $Y$-perfect matching and no $B$-perfect matching. This is equivalent to $S$ having no $Y$-perfect matching and $S$ having no $B$-perfect matching.

$S$ has no $Y$-perfect matching if there exists a non-empty set of positions $I$ such that the number of flags in $S$ having $Y$ at at least one position in $I$ is less than $|I|$.
Similarly, $S$ has no $B$-perfect matching if there exists a non-empty set of positions $J$ such that the number of flags in $S$ having $B$ at at least one position in $J$ is less than $|J|$.

Let $k = |I|$ and $l = |J|$. The condition $|N_Y(I) \cap S| < k$ implies that at least $|S| - k + 1$ flags in $S$ have $B$ at all positions in $I$. Let $S_I$ be the set of these flags. Similarly, $S_J$ is the set of flags in $S$ having $Y$ at all positions in $J$, and $|S_J| \ge |S| - l + 1$.
If $I \cap J \neq \emptyset$, then $S_I \cap S_J = \emptyset$, which leads to $|S| \le k + l - 2$.
If $I \cap J = \emptyset$, then $|S_I \cap S_J| \le 2^{8-k-l}$. By the inclusion-exclusion principle, $|S| \ge |S_I| + |S_J| - |S_I \cap S_J| \ge (|S| - k + 1) + (|S| - l + 1) - 2^{8-k-l}$.
Rearranging gives $|S| \le 2^{8-k-l} + k + l - 2$.
Maximizing this over $k, l \ge 1$ with $k+l \le 8$ yields $|S| \le 2^{8-1-1} + 1 + 1 - 2 = 64$.
Thus, the smallest $M$ is $64 + 1 = 65$.
